full_text_en:
Wu Guanzhong v. Shanghai Duoyunxuan and Hong Kong Yongcheng Antique Auction Co., Ltd. — dispute over sale of a fine art work bearing a forged signature of the plaintiff

Plaintiff: Wu Guanzhong, male, born in July 1919, professor at the Central Academy of Arts and Crafts.

Agent ad litem: Shen Zhigeng, lawyer at Beijing Zongheng Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Liu Sanhong, lawyer at Shanghai Tianren Law Firm.

Defendant: Shanghai Duoyunxuan.

Legal representative: Zhu Junbo, general manager.

Agent ad litem: Dai Xiaojing, employee of Shanghai Duoyunxuan.

Agent ad litem: Tao Wuping, lawyer at Shanghai Shenda Law Firm.

Defendant: Hong Kong Yongcheng Antique Auction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Auction Co., Ltd.).

Responsible person: Huang Hao.

Agent ad litem: Wang Yinsheng, lawyer at Shanghai Shifang Law Firm.

The plaintiff, Wu Guanzhong, filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court against the defendants Shanghai Duoyunxuan and Hong Kong Yongcheng Antique Auction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Auction Co., Ltd.) regarding a copyright dispute.

Plaintiff Wu Guanzhong alleged: On October 27, 1993, the defendants, Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., jointly auctioned in Hong Kong a painting titled "Portrait of Mao Zedong," which bore the words "Bombard the Headquarters—My Big-Character Poster, Mao Zedong," and was signed "Painted by Wu Guanzhong at the Academy of Arts and Crafts, 1962." Before the auction, Wu Guanzhong had, through relevant entities, notified Shanghai Duoyunxuan that this painting was a fake bearing his forged signature. However, after receiving the notification and written correspondence, Shanghai Duoyunxuan still proceeded with the joint auction with the Auction Co., Ltd., and even produced an expert appraisal opinion stating that it was a work by Wu Guanzhong, resulting in the fake being purchased by another party for HK$528,000. The actions of the two defendants infringed upon the plaintiff's copyright and caused undue damage to his reputation and the sale of his genuine works. Therefore, the plaintiff requested the court to order the defendants to cease the infringement, eliminate the adverse effects, make a public apology, and compensate for economic losses of HK$528,000.

The defendant Auction Co., Ltd. did not submit a defense and did not appear in court.

The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court found through public trial: The defendants, Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., signed an "Agreement" in December 1992, stipulating that they would jointly host auctions of modern Chinese calligraphy and paintings in Hong Kong in March and September 1993, and reached agreements on matters such as the selection of auction items and profit sharing. On July 27, 1993, Shanghai Duoyunxuan, as agreed, air-shipped its selected auction items to Hong Kong and dispatched personnel to preside over the appraisal, selection, and reserve price determination of auction items solicited by the Auction Co., Ltd. overseas.

On October 2, 1993, a client surnamed Zhao in Hong Kong signed a "Consignment Agreement" with the defendant Auction Co., Ltd., entrusting it to auction the painting "Portrait of Mao Zedong" bearing the signature of Wu Guanzhong; the estimated price was between HK$300,000 and HK$350,000; the remarks column stated the auction date as October 2, 1993, and provisions were made for insurance. In early October of the same year, the Auction Co., Ltd. compiled and printed a total of 382 items from its own solicitation and those provided by Shanghai Duoyunxuan into a "Catalogue," with the cover stating: "Yongcheng Antique Auction Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Duoyunxuan jointly host the 'Modern Chinese Calligraphy, Paintings, and Ancient Paintings Auction' at 2:30 p.m. on Wednesday, October 27, 1993." Item No. 231 in the Catalogue was a painting titled "Portrait of Mao Zedong" bearing the signature of Wu Guanzhong, with vertical cursive script in the upper right corner reading "Bombard the Headquarters—My Big-Character Poster, Mao Zedong," and vertical cursive script in the lower left corner reading "Painted by Wu Guanzhong at the Academy of Arts and Crafts, 1962." The dimensions were 38 cm wide and 66 cm long, with an estimated price of HK$300,000–350,000. The Auction Co., Ltd. distributed the Catalogue to the public and also provided 50 copies to Shanghai Duoyunxuan. Shortly before the auction, Shanghai Duoyunxuan gave copies of this Catalogue to relevant units and individuals in Shanghai.

In mid-October 1993, after learning of the above, the plaintiff Wu Guanzhong stated that he had never painted "Portrait of Mao Zedong" and that the creation date of 1962 was absurd. Therefore, Wu Guanzhong entrusted others to report to relevant authorities to seek the cessation of the auction of this painting. On October 25, 1993, the Shanghai Municipal Cultural Administration issued a notice (Document No. Hu Wen She Zi (93) No. 95) to Shanghai Duoyunxuan, stating: "If the 'Portrait of Mao Zedong' is indeed a forgery, it must be promptly withdrawn and the auction stopped; if there are other forgeries, they must also be handled accordingly, and you are requested to report the verification results to this office." In response, the defendant Shanghai Duoyunxuan replied: The painting was consigned to the Auction Co., Ltd. in Hong Kong; the auction would be held in Hong Kong and presided over by a Hong Kong legal entity, with the decision-making authority resting with the Auction Co., Ltd.; they would certainly convey the above opinion and the author's request to the Auction Co., Ltd. and make every effort to persuade them to withdraw the work. Subsequently, Shanghai Duoyunxuan repeatedly telegraphed its observation team in Hong Kong to convey the opinions of the relevant authorities and Wu Guanzhong to the Auction Co., Ltd., and also conducted an appraisal of the painting. After receiving the notices conveyed by Shanghai Duoyunxuan, the Auction Co., Ltd. immediately invited relevant Hong Kong experts to appraise the work, analyzing it from aspects such as creative characteristics, and concluded that Wu Guanzhong's claim of forgery was unfounded, while also confirming that the work was created in 1966 rather than 1962; they also inquired with the consignor about the purchase of the "Portrait of Mao Zedong" painting and obtained a guarantee from the consignor. The Auction Co., Ltd. also issued a certificate stating: "All matters regarding the agency, promotion, auction, etc., of the above work are handled by this company in accordance with regulations and are unrelated to Shanghai Duoyunxuan... This company can decide on the auction in accordance with Hong Kong law and the company's auction rules." In late October 1993, experts from Shanghai Duoyunxuan went to Hong Kong to participate in the auction work. On the afternoon of October 27, 1993, the joint auction of modern Chinese calligraphy, paintings, and ancient paintings hosted by the Auction Co., Ltd. and Shanghai Duoyunxuan was held at the Hong Kong Kowloon Harbourview Hotel, and "Portrait of Mao Zedong" was sold for HK$528,000, of which HK$48,000 represented the auctioneer's commission.

On June 5, 1994, the Ministry of Public Security of the People's Republic of China, at the request of Wu Guanzhong's employer, the Central Academy of Arts and Crafts, issued an appraisal regarding whether the signature on "Portrait of Mao Zedong" in the Catalogue was written by Wu Guanzhong himself. The appraisal stated: "The handwriting 'Wu Guanzhong painted at the Academy of Arts and Crafts, 1966 (duplicate character) year' on the painting is written with a brush, at a relatively slow speed, with normal handwriting and stable characteristics, suitable for examination. A comparative examination with Wu Guanzhong's own handwriting revealed that the writing styles of the two are different, and there are significant differences in the writing of the characters 'Wu, Guan, Zhong, Hua, Yu, Gong, Yi, Mei, Yuan, Yi, Jiu, Liu, Liu (duplicate character), Nian,' the positioning of strokes, the starting and ending features of strokes, and the strength of strokes, as well as word usage characteristics, reflecting different writing habits." The conclusion was: "The handwriting 'Wu Guanzhong painted at the Academy of Arts and Crafts, 1966 (duplicate character) year' on the painting 'Portrait of Mao Zedong,' bearing the signature of Wu Guanzhong, in the auction catalogue jointly auctioned by Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., is not written by Wu Guanzhong himself." On July 16, 1994, Wu Guanzhong filed a lawsuit with the court, claiming that Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd. had infringed upon his copyright.

The Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court held upon trial: The painting "Portrait of Mao Zedong" in dispute in this case bears a signature that is not that of the plaintiff Wu Guanzhong; it is a fine art work bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong. The defendants, Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., had entered into a cooperation agreement to jointly host the auction, and the Catalogue stated that it was "jointly hosted"; moreover, they jointly presided over the entire auction process in actual practice, indicating that the auction of this painting was a joint act of the two defendants. The act of auctioning calligraphy and paintings by the two defendants is a series of actions including soliciting calligraphy and paintings, printing and distributing the Catalogue, and actually conducting the auction and settlement. An auction is a special form of sale, and auctioning calligraphy and paintings is an act of selling fine art works. After being informed of the plaintiff's objection to the painting, and without conclusive evidence that the work was created by the plaintiff and that the signature was not the plaintiff's own, the two defendants nevertheless proceeded to auction and sell the painting for profit, which violates Article 46(7) of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China and constitutes an act of selling a fine art work bearing a forged signature of another person, infringing upon the copyright. Wu Guanzhong's claim that the two defendants sold a fine art work bearing his forged signature, infringing upon his copyright, has factual and legal basis and should be supported. Shanghai Duoyunxuan's defense in court that the auction was not a sale and that it was not actually a joint auctioneer of the painting lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported. The actions of Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., in ignoring warnings and insisting on jointly auctioning the fine art work "Portrait of Mao Zedong" bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong, jointly and seriously infringed upon Wu Guanzhong's copyright, causing material and moral damage. Pursuant to Articles 134(1), (7), (9), and (10) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, they shall bear joint and several civil liability for ceasing the infringement, eliminating adverse effects, making a public apology, and compensating for losses. Accordingly, on September 28, 1995, the court rendered the following judgment: 1. The joint auction by the defendant Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the defendant Auction Co., Ltd. of the painting "Portrait of Mao Zedong" bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong infringed upon the plaintiff Wu Guanzhong's copyright, and they shall cease the infringement; 2. The two defendants shall publish articles in the People's Daily (Overseas Edition) and Guangming Daily to publicly apologize to the plaintiff and eliminate adverse effects, with the content subject to review and approval by this court; 3. The two defendants shall jointly compensate the plaintiff for losses in the amount of RMB 73,000.

The first-instance litigation costs of RMB 2,700 shall be jointly borne by the defendant Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the defendant Auction Co., Ltd.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, the defendant Shanghai Duoyunxuan appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court.

The appellant Shanghai Duoyunxuan alleged in its appeal: Request the reversal of the first-instance judgment and a retrial of this case. The main facts and reasons are: The first-instance judgment contained major errors and serious inaccuracies in the finding of facts; the application of law was incorrect, as this case should not apply the law of the place where one defendant is located, but rather the "law of the place of auction," i.e., the law of Hong Kong; and it was unjust for the first-instance judgment to impose the same legal liability on Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd.

The appellee Wu Guanzhong responded: The first-instance judgment's findings of fact were clear and the application of law was correct; he requests that the second-instance court uphold the first-instance judgment and dismiss the appellant's claims.

The defendant at first instance, the Auction Co., Ltd., did not submit a written defense within the statutory period, but argued at the trial: Shanghai Duoyunxuan had repeatedly conveyed to this company the opinions of relevant authorities and the author regarding the auction of "Portrait of Mao Zedong." After consulting with the consignor and inviting relevant calligraphy and painting appraisers to conduct a comprehensive appraisal of the painting, this company made the decision to proceed with the auction. This decision was both prudent and legally effective; the focus of the dispute in this case is not the authenticity of the signature but the authenticity of the work; the auction conduct of this company occurred in Hong Kong, and all rules of conduct should be governed by Hong Kong law.

The Shanghai High People's Court held upon trial: The right of authorship on a citizen's works is protected by law, and the law prohibits the creation and sale of fine art works bearing a forged signature of another person. The painting "Portrait of Mao Zedong" in dispute in this case bears a signature that is not that of Wu Guanzhong; it is a fine art work bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong. During the second-instance trial, Researcher Zhan Chucai from the Second Research Institute of the Ministry of Public Security appeared in court as a witness and elaborated in detail on the process and conclusions of the handwriting appraisal of the signature on "Portrait of Mao Zedong." The appellant Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the defendant at first instance, the Auction Co., Ltd., in the auction jointly hosted pursuant to their agreement, publicly auctioned a fine art work bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong, jointly constituting an infringement upon Wu Guanzhong's copyright. Since one of the infringers, Shanghai Duoyunxuan, is located in Shanghai; the auction activities included the solicitation of calligraphy and paintings, the compilation and distribution of the Catalogue, and the auction settlement; copies of the Catalogue bearing the painting were partially distributed in Shanghai, making Shanghai one of the places where the infringing act occurred. Therefore, it is entirely correct to apply the law of the People's Republic of China to this case. The arguments of Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd. that "Hong Kong law should apply to this case" are unfounded. Furthermore, Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd., ignoring warnings from relevant authorities, insisted on auctioning the painting, which constituted a serious infringement, and shall bear civil liability for ceasing the infringement, making a public apology, eliminating adverse effects, and compensating for losses. The first-instance judgment correctly found the facts and applied the law. However, given that the painting was directly accepted for consignment by the Auction Co., Ltd., and that Shanghai Duoyunxuan had repeatedly conveyed the opinions of relevant authorities and the author, among other facts, the Auction Co., Ltd. bears primary responsibility for the infringing act in this case, while Shanghai Duoyunxuan, as one of the joint hosts of the auction, also bears some responsibility, and they shall bear joint and several liability.

Based on the above findings, on March 11, 1996, the Shanghai High People's Court, pursuant to Article 153(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

1. Affirm item 1 of the civil judgment (1994) Hu Zhong Min (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 109 of the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court: The joint auction by the appellant Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the defendant at first instance, the Auction Co., Ltd., of the fine art work "Portrait of Mao Zedong" bearing a forged signature of Wu Guanzhong jointly and seriously infringed upon the plaintiff Wu Guanzhong's copyright, and they shall cease the infringement;

2. Affirm item 2 of the civil judgment of the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court: The appellant Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the defendant at first instance, the Auction Co., Ltd., shall publish articles in the People's Daily (Overseas Edition) and Guangming Daily to publicly apologize to the appellee Wu Guanzhong and eliminate adverse effects, with the content subject to review and approval by this court;

3. Amend item 3 of the civil judgment (1994) Hu Zhong Min (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 109 of the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court, "The two defendants shall jointly compensate the plaintiff for losses in the amount of RMB 73,000," to read: "Shanghai Duoyunxuan and the Auction Co., Ltd. shall jointly compensate Wu Guanzhong for losses in the amount of RMB 73,000, of which Shanghai Duoyunxuan shall compensate Wu Guanzhong RMB 27,000, and the Auction Co., Ltd. shall compensate Wu Guanzhong RMB 46,000."

The litigation costs for the first and second instances total RMB 5,400, of which Shanghai Duoyunxuan shall bear RMB 2,000 and the Auction Co., Ltd. shall bear RMB 3,400.
